Taylor Swift officially became the youngest-ever member of the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame when she was formally inducted into the institution by Brad Paisley during an industry gala on Monday night in Nashville.

Swift was one of six inductees into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame this year, along with Texas troubadour Lyle Lovett, frequent Paisley collaborator Lee Thomas Miller, “Two Piña Coladas” writer Shawn Camp, “Hey! Baby” singer-songwriter Bruce Channel, and former member of Buddy Holly’s Crickets, J.I. Allison, who was inducted posthumously.
The ceremony, held at the Music City Center in downtown Nashville, also recognized Georg Strait with the Career Maker Award.

While the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, founded in 1970, has a history of all-star induction events, this year’s was particularly high-profile due to the presence of Swift. The pop superstar was in attendance on Monday night and watched as Lainey Wilson sang a stripped down acoustic version of “Love Story.”

In her induction speech, Swift called Nashville “the place that I went to in my middle school daydream” and “the place where all the wisdom that I wished to acquire existed in one place.” She added, “It’s not lost on me how crazy this is.”

This is just the latest songwriting honor for Swift. During a ceremony in New York in June, she became the youngest woman ever inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. And in 2022, she was lauded with the Songwriter-Artist of the Decade Award from the Nashville Songwriters Association International.

That Monday night’s induction took place in Nashville reinforced the global icon’s apparent return to Nashville. Earlier this summer, she scored another country radio Number One with “I Knew It, I Knew You,” her first country chart-topper since “Highway Don’t Care” in 2013. And this past August, Swift talked at length about reconnecting with her Nashville roots during a conversation with Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. for the institution’s Icon Sessions series in L.A.

“I love my country roots more and more the further along this path I get and I want to honor them more and more,” Swift said. “I feel more tied to them, more loyal to them … The people that shaped who I am as an artist and as a writer, that all happened in Nashville.”
Hubert de la Bouillerie, who edited films including George Miller’s “The Witches of Eastwick” and “Tango & Cash,” died Aug. 8 in Los Angeles. He was 75.
Among his credits was additional editing on the 1970 documentary “Woodstock,” along with “Highlander II: The Quickening,” “Mo’ Money,” “Doin’ Time,” “Blank Check” and “Celtic Pride.”
He also served as editor on “Police Academy 5” and “Police Academy 6.”

De la Bouillerie also moved behind the camera as a director. His directing credits included the 1996 television film “The Right to Remain Silent,” whose ensemble cast included Lea Thompson, LL Cool J, Patrick Dempsey, Christopher Lloyd, Amanda Plummer and Carl Reiner, as well as the 1997 science-fiction film “The Apocalypse.”

His wife, Debbie Robins de la Bouillerie, pre-deceased him. Earlier in his life, Hubert was married to Hilary Saltzman, daughter of film producer Harry Saltzman, who, together with Albert R. Broccoli, brought the original James Bond film series to the screen.
Later in his career, Hubert continued to develop his own projects as a writer and producer, reflecting the breadth of his interests and his lifelong commitment to storytelling.
He was also an accomplished photographer and writer. He published a novel, “Of Love and Evil: The Birth,” a gothic story weaving history, love, mystery and the supernatural.

Hubert’s family describes him as a storyteller at heart. “Whether working with moving images in an editing room, directing actors, developing a screenplay, looking through the lens of his camera or putting words onto a page, he was drawn throughout his life to creativity and artistic expression,” the family wrote in a statement.

De la Bouillerie is survived by his two children, Jacqueline Bell and Alexandre de la Bouillerie, as well as his sister Annie Goeke and his siblings Caroline Gruber, Juliette Glazebrook, Diane Cottrell, Helie de la Bouillerie and Alban de la Bouillerie.
Mathematically speaking, democracy is next to impossible.

That may sound like the premise of a Silicon Valley billionaire’s six-hour podcast, but it’s actually a statement about a remarkably stubborn problem: How do you translate a group of individual preferences into a single choice?

In 1785, the French mathematician and philosopher Nicolas de Condorcet discovered that a majority can sometimes vote itself into a logical loop. In elections with three or more candidates, each voter might rank the candidates in a perfectly clear and consistent way — yet when all the votes are tallied, every candidate loses in a head-to-head contest against one of their rivals. Changing the rules only gets us so far: As the economist Kenneth Arrow later proved, any method for combining individual rankings into a collective order must sacrifice at least one seemingly reasonable democratic requirement.

Now three researchers have shown that Condorcet’s 240-year-old paradox has a shape, and it’s suitably peculiar: a Klein bottle, a surface with no distinct inside or outside. The result gives mathematicians a geometric way to explore why seemingly reasonable rules for collective decision-making can become impossible to reconcile.

When there are only two choices, the will of the people is easy to divine: Barring a tie, the candidate preferred by a majority wins. Add a third contender, however, and things get weird. Suddenly, even agreeing on what it means to win becomes a problem.

You might simply elect whoever receives the most votes, as in a typical American election. But suppose Alice receives 35% of the vote, Bob 34%, and Carol 31%. Alice wins. Yet if Carol’s supporters all prefer Bob to Alice, then 65% of the electorate would rather have Bob. By one perfectly reasonable definition of majority rule, the wrong candidate has won.
Before anyone reaches for a tinfoil hat, let’s be clear: Every ballot is counted correctly. The question is what should count as winning.
One solution is to ask voters to rank the candidates, then choose whoever would defeat every rival in a head-to-head contest. But consider the following scenario:
- One-third of voters rank Alice over Bob over Carol.
- One-third rank Bob over Carol over Alice.
- One-third rank Carol over Alice over Bob.
- Alice beats Bob, because the first and third groups prefer Alice to Bob.
- Bob beats Carol, because the first and second groups prefer Bob to Carol.
- Carol beats Alice, because the second and third groups prefer Carol to Alice.
Every voter has a perfectly coherent ranking, yet together they have produced a result that runs in circles.

This is the paradox that Condorcet, a passionate believer in democracy, encountered in the late 18th century. As the secretary of the French Academy of Sciences, he’d been looking for ways to make sure the group was choosing new members fairly. (More enlightened than most, Condorcet would also question the democratic arithmetic of excluding half the population, explicitly defending women’s political rights in a 1790 essay. A few years later, during the Reign of Terror, the revolution he had supported put him in a prison cell; he was found dead two days after his arrest.)

Over the centuries, mathematicians, political scientists, and reformers have devised an astonishing variety of voting systems in hopes of breaking Condorcet’s impasse. Yet every method brings its own vulnerabilities. Change the system and you may well change the winner, even when the voters and their preferences remain exactly the same.

In 1951, the economist Kenneth Arrow showed how deep the problem ran. He sought a voting system that stayed consistent while meeting just a few simple democratic requirements. Voters should be free to rank the candidates in any order. No single voter should unilaterally dictate the outcome of an election. (Read: no kings.) If everyone prefers one option to another, the group’s ranking should reflect that preference. And the ranking of two candidates should depend only on how voters compare those two: Where voters place Carol on their ballots shouldn’t affect whether the group ranks Alice above Bob.

Each requirement sounds reasonable enough on its own. But, Arrow showed, no method can satisfy them all. “Quite often the will of the people doesn’t exist,” said Iain McLean of the University of Oxford.

Arrow’s impossibility theorem, as this result is now known, extended Condorcet’s paradox beyond majority rule, establishing a fundamental limit on how individual votes can be combined into a group decision. Different voting systems can change which of Arrow’s requirements fail, but no single system can ever preserve them all. “You have to make a choice as a system designer as to which of the conditions it’s most harmless to fail,” McLean said.

In 1980, to better understand this phenomenon, the mathematician and economist Graciela Chichilnisky turned to topology, an area of math in which shapes are considered equivalent if one can be stretched into another without tearing. In a footnote, she mused that Condorcet’s paradox in particular could be thought about as a topological problem.
Now mathematicians have proved her intuition true.
What, then, does a voting paradox look like?

To answer this question, the new work builds on a model that Yuliy Baryshnikov, now a professor at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, proposed in 1993. First, consider a single voter’s ballot in an election with three candidates. There are six possible ways to rank the options. Each one can be represented by a triangle:
Each corner of this triangle represents one of the comparisons the ballot implies: Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, and Alice over Carol.

A different ballot listing Alice first, Carol second, and Bob third agrees on two of those comparisons, since both ballots put Alice above her rivals. Their triangles therefore share two corners and can be joined along the edge connecting them.
Now join all six triangles (representing all possible ballots) along their matching edges. You get a strip:
The edges at its two ends also match. So bend the strip around and glue those edges together, matching the labels. You get a tube with an opening at each end:
Baryshnikov used this model to give a new topological proof of Arrow’s impossibility theorem.
But look at what happens at either end of the tube. Around one rim, the comparisons read Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, and Carol over Alice. Around the other, the cycle runs in reverse.

We’re left with Condorcet’s paradoxical cycles — voting results that run in circles. Baryshnikov had ignored these rims. But 30 years later, in April 2025, Ori Livson, a doctoral student at the University of Sydney, reconsidered them. After all, sometimes such circular relationships are allowed, as in the rules of rock-paper-scissors. The trouble arises in situations like elections, when those relationships are expected to form a consistent ranking. Livson wanted a topological model that could distinguish cases where the cycles are allowed from cases where they aren’t.
Together with his adviser, Mikhail Prokopenko, and Prokopenko’s longtime colleague Siddharth Pritam of the Chennai Mathematical Institute, he set out to model the troublesome case.

Each cycle around the tube’s rims leads to the same impossible conclusion: Every candidate ranks above every other. In that sense, both rims are saying the same thing. And in topology, “once you realize two things are the same, you can glue them together,” Livson said.
Srishti Saloni; Georgia Callinan; Natalia Kishigami

If you bend the tube until its two openings meet, you get a doughnut-shaped surface called a torus. But this gluing also connects individual edges from each rim in pairings that represent incompatible relationships. An edge representing “Bob over Alice over Carol,” for instance, gets glued to an edge representing “Bob over Carol over Alice.” The researchers needed a way to join the rims without creating such contradictions.

The solution? A twist. Instead of matching one rim to the other point by point, in the same order, the twist allowed the researchers to reverse the order of preferences around one of the rims — making the cycles equivalent. “Gluing with the twist is the only valid option,” Livson said.

If you twist a strip of paper and join its edges, you get a surface with only one side, called a Möbius strip. But what happens when you twist a tube? You end up with something remarkable and strange: a Klein bottle.

Like a Möbius strip, a Klein bottle has only one side, with no distinct inside or outside. Unlike a Möbius strip, it has no edge. (If it looks as if this surface crosses itself, it does — in three dimensions. Mathematicians avoid this by constructing the Klein bottle in four dimensions, where it can close up without self-intersecting.)

The trio had their model. Just as each voter can supply a coherent ranking, and yet the electorate’s preferences refuse to fit into a single order, each small patch of a Klein bottle appears to have two sides, yet those sides cannot be distinguished consistently across the whole surface. In both cases, something that makes sense piece by piece breaks down when we try to put the pieces together.

For Livson, Pritam, and Prokopenko, that resemblance raises a larger question: Can topology help explain other fundamental limits on what mathematics can accomplish? Perhaps these different impossibilities, when given a shape, will turn out to share a deeper geometric explanation.

Topology makes the paradox tangible, but choosing a voting system still means picking your poison. Mathematics can tell us what the trade-offs entail. Our priorities determine which ones are worth making. And that’s something no theorem can settle for us. “It’s not really a mathematical debate,” McLean said. “It’s a debate about values.”
New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
- University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, News Bureau

- Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.

Scientists have developed and tested the first three-dimensional thermal invisibility cloak, a device that can conceal objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme temperatures. The breakthrough could lead to new ways to cool microchips, safeguard delicate electronics, and prevent equipment from being detected through its thermal signature.

The cloak can conceal objects with a wide variety of shapes, regardless of the direction from which heat approaches. Earlier thermal cloaks were limited to two dimensions or worked only when heat traveled in a particular direction. The new design overcomes these restrictions by directing heat around a hidden object rather than simply blocking it. As a result, infrared imaging shows a temperature pattern that makes the object appear to be absent.

The research was conducted by University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign civil and environmental engineering professor Shelly Zhang, postdoctoral researcher Weichen Li, and graduate student Yibo Wang, in collaboration with professor Ole Sigmund of the Technical University of Denmark. Their findings were published in Nature Communications.

"A real thermal cloak should work no matter where the heat comes from," Zhang said. "Our device can hide a complex 3D object in an infinite number of directions while keeping the temperature inside stable and protected."
A New Material Makes 3D Thermal Invisibility Possible

Creating a thermal cloak that functions in three dimensions has been a longstanding challenge. Previous experimental devices could redirect heat only across a flat surface or along one direction of heat flow, leaving them far short of the capabilities needed for a fully three-dimensional cloak.

To overcome these limitations, the researchers revisited the foundational principles of transformation thermotics, a field that explores how heat can be redirected through specially designed materials. They focused on a central question: "What kind of material structure could cover almost all the thermal properties needed for a perfect cloak?"

The solution was a new lattice-based material whose structure can be independently adjusted along three directions. These changes allow the researchers to control how efficiently heat passes through different parts of the cloak. Compared with previous designs, the material can achieve a much broader range of thermal conductivities, closely approaching the properties predicted to be necessary for ideal thermal cloaking.

Importantly, the researchers went beyond computer simulations and constructed a working device. They used 3D metal printing to produce an intricate aluminum lattice, which provides pathways for efficient heat conduction. They then used mold casting to fill the remaining spaces with a rubber-like material that conducts heat poorly. Together, these materials create a structure that can carefully control the movement of heat.
Infrared Camera Tests Confirm the Cloak Works

To evaluate the device, the team positioned it between hot and cold regions, establishing a temperature difference that caused heat to flow through the surrounding environment. They monitored the resulting temperature patterns with an infrared camera to determine whether the cloak could successfully redirect heat around the concealed area.

The experiments showed that the device could guide heat around the hidden region while preserving the surrounding temperature pattern. To an infrared camera, the area appeared much as it would if no object were present. At the same time, temperatures inside the cloak remained uniform, shielding the concealed space from the extreme conditions outside.

The researchers also tested whether the cloak could accommodate unusually complicated objects. They successfully concealed intricate three-dimensional geometries, including detailed shapes resembling human heads. According to the team, earlier experimental thermal cloaks have not demonstrated a comparable combination of geometric complexity and cloaking performance.
Potential Applications in Electronics and Stealth Technology

The ability to control heat in three dimensions could have important implications across several industries. In electronics, the technology could help engineers direct heat away from sensitive components, improve thermal management in microchips, and protect devices operating under demanding conditions.

The researchers also see potential applications in security and defense. Future versions of the technology might help conceal people or equipment from thermal detection systems or shield valuable assets from severe temperature conditions. These uses would build on the device's demonstrated ability to redirect external heat while keeping the protected region thermally stable.

"Any field that needs precise control of heat or needs to protect something from being detected thermally could benefit from this work," Zhang said. "But we also see it more broadly: it's about hiding and protecting information that is carried by heat."
The Next Challenge Is Hiding Objects That Generate Heat

Although the current cloak represents a major advance, the researchers want to develop more sophisticated versions capable of performing additional functions. One particularly important goal is to conceal objects that produce heat themselves, rather than only protecting them from heat originating outside the cloak.

Achieving this would require materials that can actively control heat within the concealed region. Instead of simply redirecting incoming heat, a future cloak would need to concentrate, distribute, or guide thermal energy as conditions change. Such capabilities could expand the technology's usefulness in electronics, thermal protection, and applications involving infrared detection.

"We've shown that a true 3D omnidirectional thermal cloak is possible," Zhang said. "The next step is to make cloaks that don't just hide and protect, but also actively manipulate heat in useful ways."

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Villum Foundation, and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. Zhang is also affiliated with mechanical science and engineering and the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more “major” discoveries in math, computer science, and physics. What’s different this time is the choice to have external experts that OpenAI describes as “shepherds” guiding the results in computer science and physics, while for the math problem it says that they advised it to release the AI output for researchers to work through their own explanations.
OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
This time OpenAI says it’s taking new advice from scientists on how to release the results.

The physics information has not been released in full, but is a “mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.” According to OpenAI, “David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.”

The computer science collaboration is said to prove that the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which has been widely believed to be true, is actually false. OpenAI says verification of the result will be guided by a group of three experts that includes UC San Diego’s Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who were part of the group that originally proposed it in 1999, as well as MIT professor Ryan Williams. You don’t hear the defenders of so-called western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.

Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.

Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, King of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.

“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”

Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialogue, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: the Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user. “Fire that person.”

But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey. He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.

So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey, not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”

The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”

In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “The Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”

Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does.

The Bank of Japan is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at the end of its two-day meeting on Friday, according to a CNBC survey, with the possibility of a hike very much alive in the coming months.

All 16 respondents expect the BOJ to stand pat, given the bank raised rates last month to their highest level in 31 years. All respondents said they expect the BOJ to set the stage for a rate hike in December or January next year, as domestic inflation and wages continue to rise.

Macroeconomic factors support the BOJ's additional policy tightening, said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier. "But there may not be sufficient consensus in the policy board for successive rate hikes given the fragility in the domestic bond market," he added.
Sosuke Nakamura, an economist at Citi Research, said he sees no clear signs of inflation accelerating to a degree that would justify consecutive rate hikes.

Japan's core inflation, excluding fresh foods, for September rose 2.1% from a year earlier, reaching its highest this year as a weak yen raises import costs and elevated energy costs feed through to higher prices, even as government subsidies absorb rising costs of energy for consumers.

Japan's inflation-adjusted wages rose for the eighth month in a row in August, climbing 1.5% from a year earlier, according to the most recent government data, signaling potential wage-growth-driven inflation as well.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly told lawmakers last week that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also pushing up prices.
The BOJ is expected to declare that its "underlying inflation" target of 2% has been met at this meeting, according to reports by Reuters and The Japan Times.

Ryutaro Kimura, senior fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said he was waiting to see if the BOJ changes its phrasing about inflation in the monetary policy statement this week from "underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent" to it "has reached 2 percent."

As for the yen, nine respondents expect it to trade between 157 and 158 against the greenback over the next one month. Respondents' outlook for the three-month yen target was more scattered, ranging from 150 to 160.

"BOJ normalization, higher domestic yields and shifting institutional flows should gradually narrow the rate differential and pull capital back toward Japan," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management. But he added, "Elevated U.S. yields should prevent a straight-line yen rally."

The yen strengthened against the dollar, and Japanese government bond yields fell last week due to safe-haven demand amid a sell-off in AI stocks — a reversal from earlier in the month, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's spending plans and a global bond sell-off pressured those assets.

Nine respondents said they expect the yield on the benchmark 10-year JGBs to be between 3% and 3.1% by the end of the year, up from the current 2.809%. Seven respondents said they expect the yield on the 30-year JGB to rise to 4% to 4.1% from 3.829% as of Tuesday.
That forecast comes as analysts expect the BOJ will resume tightening after an anticipated pause in October.

Takuji Aida, chief Japan economist at Credit Agricole, said the next rate hike is likely to happen in January, when the BOJ is scheduled to release its quarterly outlook report that assesses economic activity and prices.
Thirteen respondents said they expect a terminal rate, or the level at which the BOJ is expected to stop its tightening cycle, of 1.75% to 2% by around mid-2027.

Macroeconomic data shows the policy rate is closer to the neutral level of 2%, the BOJ's inflation target, said Masato Koike, senior economist at SOMPO Institute Plus. But "given the state of the Japanese economy and the need to avoid excessive downward pressure on growth, I expect the BOJ to stop raising rates at around 1.75%," Koike said.
The CNBC survey was conducted from Oct. 14 to 26 among 16 economists and analysts.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie and Sri Jegarajah contributed to this report.
Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud

In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars, the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards.

In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts. Most SNAP cards rely on a magnetic stripe for swipe payment – which tends to be vulnerable to skimming because it does a poor job of securing the data stored on cards.

Many banks in the U.S. took action against this issue over a decade ago by upgrading their cards to include microchips and tap-to-pay, which are considered more secure. But states have lagged in making such a transition for Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards, which are what SNAP recipients use to access food aid. Currently, fewer than a third of states have made the switch or are in process of doing so, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Now, under the proposed rule released by the USDA last week, all states would have to adopt chip-enabled EBT cards. It also requires retailers that accept SNAP benefits to have payment terminals that support tap-pay. The USDA's Food and Nutrition Administration, which administers SNAP, attributed card skimming as a reason behind the proposal.
"These proposed changes will protect SNAP benefits from thieves and ensure benefits are accessible by approved households," the Food and Nutrition Administration said in its summary of the rule.

Back in January, the USDA Office of Inspector General projected that SNAP theft could climb to $233 million between 2025 and 2026 — largely as a result of skimming. A recent ProPublica investigation found that last year, $470 million was stolen electronically from SNAP recipients. The total was calculated using data from Propel, an app that helps SNAP recipients check their food benefits.
In most states, stolen benefits are not replaced — leaving recipients to make difficult choices, such as skipping meals or borrowing money in order to pay for groceries, according to Propel.

Earlier this month, NPR reported that food assistance card modernization had widespread support from state officials and federal watchdogs, as well as Republicans and Democrats in Congress. But money has been a major barrier for states to make the switch. According to the Government Accountability Office, chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than their magnetic strip counterparts.

The federal push for stronger card security features comes as state SNAP agencies are facing new budget pressures triggered by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The proposed regulation recognized the financial barrier, adding that the USDA is interested in hearing from state agencies about the cost burden.
"As stewards of taxpayer dollars, the Department considers these administrative costs as a necessary investment to deter the loss of Federally-funded SNAP benefits," the proposed rule said.

The public has 60 days to submit comments on the proposal before the USDA publishes a final rule. The department is considering giving states a two-year deadline from that publication date to implement the rule, but it also welcomed input on whether that's enough time.

When asked if the department would consider providing funding to help states upgrade their card technology, the USDA said that "For years, States had access to administrative funds to stop this egregious abuse of taxpayer resources. Yet few acted."
The USDA added that the proposed rule has been in the works for nearly four years. It estimates that the changes will reduce stolen benefits by at least $1.5 billion over the next decade.

SNAP has been one of the focus areas in the Trump administration's war on fraud. Last week, the Justice Department announced that its fraud division helped uncover nearly $42 million in schemes targeting food benefits. The investigations ranged from identity theft to retailers illegally exchanging cash for food benefits.

An A/C complaint used to mean an uncomfortable customer. On a vehicle whose thermal system also helps cool batteries, power electronics and other critical components, it can mean compromised performance—or a vehicle that cannot complete the trip. The responsibility has changed. Gary DeLuca believes the industry’s approach to diagnosing the system is overdue for a change, too.

Autel is taking on that challenge with the new MaxiHVAC AC909 Advanced A/C Diagnostic System and a full day of advanced HVAC and thermal-management training on Friday, October 30, in Port Washington, New York. For technicians and educators, the event offers a rare opportunity to learn directly from DeLuca, the Autel U.S. founder who spearheaded the tool’s development, and understand the diagnostic strategy behind it. Join Autel’s advanced HVAC training October 30, 8 a.m.–6 p.m., at the Hilton Garden Inn Roslyn in Port Washington, NY. Tickets are $249, including meals. Seating is limited. Register at autel.cc/hvac-training-ny.
“The training and the testing equipment needed to properly diagnose these HVAC, now thermal-management systems have not kept up with the technology over the last 25 years,” DeLuca said.

For a technician facing a difficult cooling complaint, that gap means more time spent trying to reconcile gauge readings, scan data and component behavior. For a shop owner, it can mean an unresolved repair, another comeback or advanced work leaving the shop. Autel’s answer is to bring the precision and diagnostic discipline of commercial HVAC into automotive service—and put the technician’s understanding of the system at the center of the process.

This is familiar territory for Autel. The company has built a history of industry disruption by challenging established ways of working and putting more capability into technicians’ hands. Its TPMS tools have simplified sensor programming and relearns. Its diagnostic tablets have expanded independent shops’ access to vehicle information and testing. Its camera-based ADAS positioning systems have brought guided optical measurement to the demanding work of calibration setup. Each advancement has helped shops take on increasingly complex service with greater confidence.

DeLuca has been part of that work throughout. He led Autel U.S. through its formative years and has contributed his repair and teaching experience to the engineering and development of Autel’s tools and diagnostic tablets. His understanding of what happens in the bay has helped shape what those tools test, how they present information and how they guide the technician toward a repair decision.

DeLuca first crossed paths with Autel’s future global leadership at industry events and trade shows and began working with them to develop products built around technicians’ real-world needs. The company’s beginnings were modest: Autel U.S. launched in 2011 with a handful of employees. DeLuca helped build that operation into a growing diagnostic-tool company, grounding its development in the needs of working technicians.

His own foundation was the repair shop. DeLuca began working in his father’s shop at age 12, earned an Automotive Technology degree from Morrisville College, and spent more than 40 years as a shop owner and trainer. With more than 50 years of automotive repair and education experience, including A/C and commercial HVAC, he brings both technical knowledge and a teacher’s determination to make it useful.
“At my core, I am a teacher and an educator. My success is based on change, and if we don’t change, we are not going to go forward,” said DeLuca.

That outlook drove the AC909 from initial concept through the development of a functioning system. Technicians were telling DeLuca they needed help finding the cause of difficult complaints, locating leaks and reducing comebacks. Meanwhile, the systems themselves were becoming more demanding: variable-displacement and electric compressors, electronically controlled expansion valves, chillers, heat exchangers and multiple thermal circuits. Depending on the vehicle, thermal management can serve the cabin, battery, inverter, drive motor and heat-sensitive electronics.

“A complete professional A/C service goes far beyond refrigerant removal, recycling and recharging,” DeLuca said. Refrigerant-handling equipment performs an essential service function. Finding the cause of a performance problem requires another level of investigation: understanding how pressures, temperatures, airflow and electronic controls affect one another. That is the diagnostic skill Autel set out to strengthen with the AC909.

A compressor may be underperforming because of an internal fault, an electrical problem or the command it is receiving. A cabin cooling complaint may involve airflow or blend-door operation even when the refrigerant circuit is functioning. The technician needs to see both what the vehicle is asking the system to do and what the system is actually doing. The AC909 connects those two sides of the diagnosis.

The AC909 was developed to give technicians the measurements and system insight needed to make those decisions. Refrigerant pressures, temperatures, humidity and other physical measurements appear alongside supported vehicle diagnostic data on a single graphical analysis screen. Illustrated procedures and dedicated component tests help technicians evaluate operation, isolate faults and verify the repair. The approach pairs guided testing with the information technicians need to understand why a result matters and what to investigate next.

DeLuca’s strategy considers four connected areas: the electrical, refrigerant, air and coolant loops. That means checking vehicle modules for trouble codes and relevant live data, evaluating refrigerant-system efficiency, verifying airflow and blend-door operation, and considering coolant temperatures and operating conditions where applicable.

The AC909D package also brings commercial HVAC testing practices into the automotive workflow. A Bluetooth-enabled NAVAC vacuum pump and digital micron gauge provide live vacuum measurements on the tablet. Micron measurement and decay testing give technicians a measurable basis for evaluating evacuation and system readiness. Nitrogen and forming gas testing accurately support leak diagnosis before charging.

The goal is a repair process technicians can follow from the initial complaint through final verification. For shop owners, that means an opportunity to reduce unnecessary parts replacement and repeated labor, use refrigerant more carefully and equip their teams to retain more demanding thermal-management work.

The response has reinforced the need for training. DeLuca describes interest in the AC909 as “phenomenal,” with technicians and college instructors traveling from across the country to attend. In evaluations at Pittsburg State University, faculty and students benchmarked properly operating systems and tested vehicles with poor A/C performance. Scott Norman, professor and Automotive Technology Program Coordinator, described the AC909 as “like going from DOS to Windows” and “a huge game changer in the automotive industry.”

On October 30, DeLuca will teach the approach behind that change. The program will cover vehicle data and physical measurements, pressure and temperature relationships, humidity analysis, component testing, new leak-detection techniques, and thermal-management strategies for conventional vehicles, hybrids and EVs, including heat pumps.

That same emphasis on understanding will guide the training. Attendees will learn how to connect a test result to system behavior and a repair decision. For DeLuca, restoring the diagnostic discipline of A/C service and preparing technicians for modern thermal management are part of the same job: teaching people to measure, analyze, repair and verify with confidence.
“This event will start the new era of change,” he said.
For an industry already experiencing that change in its service bays, Autel is bringing the tool, the strategy and the people behind its development together in one room.

The training runs from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. in the Grand Ballroom at the Hilton Garden Inn Roslyn, 3 Harbor Park Drive, Port Washington, New York. The Maria Bamford Questionnaire is a series of 25 questions designed by the beloved comedian to unearth surprising truths about its respondents. In this edition, you’ll learn about Quinta Brunson, the Emmy-winning creator and star of Abbott Elementary, which kicked off its sixth season on October 7.
What do you like to eat and/or drink right before bed?

I don’t really eat before bed, but I like to drink. Usually a cannabis drink that helps with sleep. There’s a company called Cann that has a lovely drink that helps me go down. I try to time it so that I don’t feel the effects of being high. I just want it to help me stay asleep. It’s usually one of those or just water.
What would your religion be like if you could make up your own?
Everyone would be right. I think that would solve a lot of issues. No one would be wrong about who they think God is or what they think the right dogma is. Everyone’s right — deal with it.
If you had to be the face of a product, what would you choose?

I love a honey-roasted turkey slice. It’s great protein. It’s a wonderful midday snack — add some cheese, a little bit of mustard, a little bit of mayo, and you will feel like you had an entire sandwich. There’s not a good advocate out there for honey-roasted turkey slices, so I think I could put my full faith behind it. Not a specific brand or company, just the concept of a honey-roasted turkey slice. It almost hits like caffeine. You think you have no energy, and then you have that honey-roasted turkey slice. Game changer.
What’s your most repetitive, long-term fear?

That my cooking will kill someone or make someone sick. It hasn’t happened, but I’m also scared that maybe it has happened and the person just didn’t tell me. I’ve had that fear since I was a young girl and started cooking. Chicken is so temperamental. Beef you can eat well, medium well, rare. Same thing with fish. If chicken isn’t cooked properly, everyone could be in deep trouble, but it’s definitely the thing I make the most.

There’s a recipe I make that’s kind of been passed down to me from my mom. It doesn’t sound like much, but for some reason, it hits. It’s adobo seasoning, garlic powder, and pepper. You season one side of the chicken, foil the pan, put it in the oven for 20 to 30 minutes, take it out, and season the other side of the chicken the same. I think my unbridled fear helps me make sure that it’s done right.

I was on Live With Kelly and Mark right before this. Morning shows are so different from late-night television or sitcoms. They have their own rhythm. Things you think are silly are actually so entertaining on a morning show. There was some guy dancing, and I was like, This is incredible. Waking up to do those shows is so hard, and they do it every day. They know you probably just got off a flight and have had no sleep, so they do a really good job of working with you and making sure you’re exciting for the audience. Those are America’s people right there. Everyone loves the morning people, and I think there’s a real skill in that.
What is the last thing you read — labels, Us Weekly, and texts count. Can you give us the gist of what you learned?

The last thing I read was an article about the psychology of sports betting and gambling and its connection to us now buying these mystery-box items. There’s this connection between Americans’ lack of control right now and leaving their fates in the hands of others. People are enjoying the thrill-seeking of I don’t know what’s in the box. Just give it to me. It was talking about how interesting it is that people are using sports betting as their financial plan right now. That’s kind of nuts, but that’s where we are. It’s so different from where we were even ten years ago.

We had an Abbott story line dedicated to it last year that was totally my doing just because I think for a while people didn’t realize with sports betting that they were betting. They just thought they were doing something fun on their phone, the way it was being presented to them. But you’re doing the same thing as going into a casino, if not even more dangerous because it’s right there on your phone. I am really nervous about children doing it — and many of them are — and the effect it has on how they look at money, finances, and gambling. You used to have to be 21 to do it, but now it’s happening earlier and earlier. I’m just going to hope for the best.

I’ve never bought a used thing. This isn’t to say that I wouldn’t. When I was younger, I worked at Apple, so I would get a nice discount on a new computer or a new phone. If anything, I always just saved up to buy something new. But if I get the opportunity to buy a ’67 Mustang, that’s something that I would do and that would be used.
Who was the most difficult person to listen to (for you) recently?

There was a bathroom at a gas station I went to one time somewhere in Jersey. You want to say “Never say never,” but I remember that gas station and I remember that bathroom and I will never go back into that bathroom. Just disgusting. There was blood on the wall! And other things! I made this assumption: This is not a “flag the establishment” kind of place. It was more like “You need to get out of here, Yankee.” That’s the energy I felt in that bathroom. It was on me. I had no business in that part of town. I should’ve got gas before I left New York. I won’t name the establishment because I don’t want to taint their business, but you won’t see me in there again.
If you were without home or ability to earn, do you have anyone you can turn to for shelter and financial support? For how long?

Absolutely. Many, many people. I feel like I have a good amount of family and a good amount of friends. I could pull up on anybody in a minute, and I think they knew, if I needed that, that something has gone really wrong.
What TV show or movie would you want to play a part in and what part would it be?

I’m watching VisionQuest on Disney+, and I think it’s a fun show. They’re doing this balance of serious and comedy — it’s a fun world that I would have a good time playing around in. I’ve been a huge Marvel fan my whole life. I’m hoping to hop off the train once Doomsday comes out. This has been years of my life and I’m ready to free myself of the MCU.

But there are also different characters in different worlds. There’s a DC character named Etta Candy who’s in the Wonder Woman world. Squirrel Girl has always been interesting to me. When I was younger, I was really interested in playing Ironheart, but I aged out of that; I was a big fan of the comics. I’m a huge Iron Man girl, so if ever there was a reason — which there never would be — for me to be Iron Man, I would love that.
What’s something you’d like to quit — a substance, a habit, etc. — and how would you go about it?

I have a horrible habit of biting my cheeks. I don’t know why I picked it up. I haven’t brought it up to a therapist yet, but I know it’s a nervous thing. Fortunately, I don’t bite them until I bleed or anything like that. I’ve been going to a dentist, and they’re like, “A lot of people do it!” But I’d like to quit it because sometimes I’ll watch myself on something and see myself biting my cheeks and I just can’t stand it. I have no plan to quit right now, but I think when life slows down a bit, I’ll quit then.
If you could take a brain ride in anyone’s consciousness, whose would it be?

My nephew is 10 years old, and the way he is taking the world in is really fascinating to me. He’s not a big talker and I love that about him, so I would like to be there for his thought process. He had a little role on my show recently. He’s not a kid that’s like “Yeah!” or in your face, but his mom told me that they had a little watch party for him, which he didn’t ask for, and when he got in the car to go to the little watch party, he had on cologne. They were like, “Are you wearing cologne?” And he said, “Yes.” And I just want to know what made his little brain go, Big occasion. I need to put on cologne for this, and then not tell anyone.
What is something you regret doing within the past week?

I had wine. My parents aren’t big drinkers, but my dad got a bunch of alcohol for his retirement party as gifts and they’re never gonna drink it, so my sisters and I decided to have some. It was good wine, but I shouldn’t have done that. That was, like, three days ago, and I’m still hurting.
What are you jealous of in a family member?

My older brother is able to talk his way in and out of anything. I wouldn’t say jealous, but I’m enamored by that. It’s something that I can’t do. I think too much about everybody’s thoughts and feelings, and he’s not like that. I’ve seen him do it. It’s really fascinating, the things he should not be able to talk his way out of that he does.

I would safely say three. My regular brown, this color we’ve got going on right now — but this has been phased, so it’s been, like, five different colors — and red. When I was in school, I did the classic reddish, auburnish hair all the Black girls were doing. Super fly, by the way. But I’m not a big hair-color girl. I’m a serious woman. I can’t just be out here doing pinks and blues and stuff like that. I made that decision when I was really young. I was like, You’re serious. We have to have serious hair colors.
If you had to move anywhere outside the U.S., where would you go?

London. I do well over there. I get along well with the people, I love the environment, and I have a good time. Because I’m from Philadelphia, I have a real appreciation for old architecture. The older the architecture, the better. If not London, I would say Montréal. I’ve been there many times over the years for festivals and just to visit, and I think it’s a beautiful city. It’s so diverse, and I feel really happy in Montréal, so there, too.
What’s the best thing you’ve ever learned from someone you don’t like?

I used to believe that if you gave people the resources they needed to be better, they would be better. I don’t believe that anymore, unfortunately. It’s up to the individual to make a choice to be better. I learned that recently from a person that … I wouldn’t say I don’t like, but I wanted to help. It’s hard for me to straight-up not like a person. I think everybody’s doing the best they can with what they’ve got.
What did you have for breakfast this morning, and is it your usual?

It’s not my usual. Whenever I come to Philly or New York, I get Dunkin’ Donuts because we didn’t have it in L.A. for a long time. Now we do, but I feel like it’s not as solid as it is here. So I had an egg and cheese on a croissant with a Dunkin’ coffee and I was so happy. That was my order when I was in high school.

At home, I make my own breakfast. I’m on set most of the time in L.A., so I’m usually getting two eggs fried, half an avocado, and ten blackberries, ten raspberries, and some blueberries, if I’m feeling funky, with Greek yogurt. It’s a nice power breakfast. Gives me enough protein to start the day, enough fiber, all that kind of crap.
Describe something that was funny to you.

It was something the makeup artist working with me said in the car today. We were having a conversation about stalkers and the various instances we’ve all heard about and encountered and she wasn’t saying much until we got to Selena. She spoke up from the back of the car and was like, “The woman who killed Selena is still a large villain in the Latin community.”

I don’t know why that was funny to me. She didn’t say it in a funny way, but it took me out. It gave me so much insight in that moment: Okay, good to know that that’s what it is in the Latin community. I also learned something about her — I didn’t know she was Latina until that moment. When someone says one sentence and I get a whole picture painted, that’s funny to me.
Describe something that is not funny to you.

Pranks. I think it’s low humor. I don’t like jokes where other people aren’t in on it. I’m like, You spent your time pranking a person or figuring out how to prank a person? You could have read a book. You could have helped solve world hunger. I’ve been pranked and I’m not saying that I’ve even hated it when it happened. But I’m just like, That’s a waste of time.
Describe something that is beautiful to you.

When I see someone help someone they don’t know — little stuff, like on a plane when someone else helps someone put their bag up in the storage bin or when someone holds a door for someone or when someone just sees someone struggling and helps them because they can. Going back to the religious idea, those are little godlike moments to me. That’s the kind of stuff that really makes the world go round.

Selfishness. It’s something that everyone goes through. You have to figure out how to be selfless while caring for yourself. But true selfishness, where you don’t care about who has to suffer in order for you to get what you get? It’s a very ugly trait.
How much money do you think is “enough” for the whole rest of your life — that you wouldn’t need to work again?

I think if you would have asked me that when I was a kid, I would’ve been like, “Whoa, $4,000!” So the number just changes as you get older. I can tell you what I have right now feels like enough. That could change tomorrow. I don’t know what will happen in my life to make me be like, Oh man, unfortunately, now I need some more money. You always think you need more, and that’s part of part of living in a capitalistic society. And the truth of the matter is that you might because it just keeps going. It’s the reason why people who make millions of dollars feel like they don’t have enough, because of lifestyle changes and economy changes. So I try not to get caught up in that and just be grateful for what I have.
What do you think is your most likely cause of death?
I hope it’s old age. Really old age. Super old. Mad old. Whatever they want to give me — I don’t know who they is — but whatever they got for me, I’ll take.
